The larval development of Austrominius modestus proceeds through a series of well-defined nauplius stages before the cypris larva becomes competent to settle. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the interval from birth to the completion of the pelagic phase is approximately 10.6 days , with roughly 8.6 days allocated to the six nauplius instars and about 2 days spent as a non-feeding cyprid. Upon settlement, the newly attached individual has a dry weight of only 0.00000581 grams , reflecting the substantial metabolic costs incurred during the protracted planktonic dispersal phase. The energy content at this critical transition point has been measured at 0.1425 joules , a value that represents the residual endogenous reserves available to fuel the initial post-settlement metamorphosis and the construction of the juvenile shell. These early benthic individuals must rapidly commence filter feeding to replenish their depleted energy stores before beginning sustained somatic growth.

Following successful attachment, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a period of rapid size increase. The time elapsed since settlement at which the first signs of reproductive maturation become apparent is 39 days [tp = 39 days], a duration that reflects the energetic requirements of reaching a threshold body size at puberty. at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]The basal diameter of the shell at this onset of sexual maturity has been documented at 0.6 centimeters [Lp = 0.6 centimeters], a size that correlates with the development of functional ovarioles and the capacity for copulation. During this juvenile phase, the growing barnacle molts and expands its calcareous wall plates, gradually increasing its feeding radius and filtering capacity. Field surveys of intertidal populations in New Zealand indicate that the ultimate basal diameter attained by fully grown individuals, representing the asymptotic adult size under typical environmental conditions, reaches 1.4 centimeters [Li = 1.4 centimeters]. This maximum dimension is rarely achieved in dense aggregations where space competition limits lateral expansion.

Reproductive output in Austrominius modestus is characterized by iteroparous brooding. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], an adult female with a basal diameter of approximately 13.5 millimeters produces roughly 2 milligrams of egg mass per brood, which translates into a clutch on the order of 2,220 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 2,220 eggs per brood]. Given the normal brooding interval of about 14 days between successive egg masses, the effective reproductive frequency is approximately one brood every 14 days [F_R_i = approximately one brood every 14 days]. This pattern of continuous, synchronized brooding during the warmer months allows a single female to generate many thousands of offspring over the course of a single reproductive season. The timing and intensity of this reproductive effort are moderated by local food availability and the energetic demands of maintaining the adult body mass during periods of elevated metabolic activity.

The relationship between body size and somatic mass in this species has been quantified through laboratory rearing studies. For an individual attaining a basal diameter of 1.35 centimeters, which corresponds closely to the ultimate size class, the measured ultimate soma dry weight is 0.033 grams , while the corresponding wet weight reaches 0.137 grams [Wwi = 0.137 grams]. This substantial investment in structural tissue supports both the feeding apparatus and the reproductive organs. At the opposite end of the life history, the wet weight at birth, derived from the volume of the fertilized egg which has a diameter of approximately 120 micrometers, is estimated at 0.0000009 grams [Wwb = 0.0000009 grams]. The contrast between this minuscule initial mass and the adult body weight underscores the dramatic degree of somatic growth that must occur within the constraints of the intertidal environment, where feeding time is limited by tidal immersion cycles.

The overall pace of the life cycle at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] is characterized by a maximum natural lifespan of approximately 511 days [am = approximately 511 days], a duration that aligns with the typical annual turnover observed in temperate barnacle populations subject to wave action and predation pressure. Senescence in this species is accompanied by a gradual decline in feeding efficiency and shell maintenance, leading to eventual dislodgement or overgrowth by competing organisms. When considering the complete sequence from the brooded egg to reproductive maturity, the larval duration of approximately 10.6 days  from birth to settlement at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] represents a relatively condensed planktonic phase compared to some other thoracican barnacles, potentially facilitating higher local recruitment rates. The post-settlement interval of 39 days [tp = 39 days] required to reach full reproductive competence further constrains the generation time, ensuring that the species can complete multiple overlapping cohorts within a single favorable growing season in New Zealand's coastal waters at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].
